clue.text: Game over for hawk

indicators.note: something turned over ends up facing the other way, so the word before is read backwards

parts.note: golf is a game played with clubs

explanation.surface: A falconer declares the hunt finished for the hawk.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hawk' looks like the bird from the surface, but here it is the verb meaning to peddle goods.
explanation.definitionFit: To hawk is to sell goods by calling out, and to flog is the informal British word for selling.

clue.text: Discovered this could make do fun?

parts.note: surface reading: a remark that something could make an activity enjoyable
setter's reading: the answer's first word is the anagram of 'do fun', and its second word is itself an anagram signal

explanation.surface: A discovery that might liven up a party.
explanation.walkthrough: A reverse clue: read the answer as a clue, a five-letter word followed by an anagram signal, and solving it gives 'do fun'.
explanation.definitionFit: To be discovered doing something wrong is to have been caught or detected, the idiomatic sense of the phrase.

clue.text: Start working hard and fast

parts.note: a machine that is working is on
set and hard-and-fast both mean fixed and firm

explanation.surface: Beginning to work hard and quickly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hard and fast' reads as two ways of working, but it is one idiom meaning rigid or fixed.
explanation.definitionFit: The onset of something is its beginning or start, as in the onset of winter.

clue.text: Pubs without stress — places for regulars

indicators.note: without in its old sense of outside, so the pubs sit around the other word

parts.note: bars are pubs
to rack is to strain or stress

explanation.surface: Relaxed pubs are the haunts of the regular drinkers.
explanation.walkthrough: Regulars are not pub-goers here but regular soldiers, members of the standing army.
explanation.definitionFit: Barracks are the buildings where regular soldiers live and are housed.

clue.text: Possibly Audrey Hepburn's wonderful short hair

indicators.note: short means cut off before the end, so the word drops its last letter

parts.note: ace means excellent or wonderful
a tress is a lock of hair

explanation.surface: Praise for Audrey Hepburn's famous short haircut.
explanation.walkthrough: Hepburn's pixie cut in Roman Holiday makes 'short hair' read as one phrase; 'short' belongs to 'wonderful'.
explanation.definitionFit: Audrey Hepburn was a film star, so she is one example of a female performer; 'Possibly' marks the example.

clue.text: Yank chain up and down a lot

parts.note: rocky means unsteady, going up and down
mountains of something means a great deal of it

explanation.surface: Instructions to jerk a chain repeatedly up and down.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Yank chain' reads as pulling a chain; Yank is slang for American and the chain is a mountain range.
explanation.definitionFit: The Rocky Mountains are the major mountain range of western North America, an American chain of peaks.

clue.text: Got a clue muddled penning a list

indicators.note: penning means shutting in, like animals in a pen, so the letters enclose the small word
muddled means jumbled up, so the letters of those words are mixed into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: A confused solver writing out a list after getting a clue muddled.
explanation.definitionFit: A catalogue is a systematic list of items, such as goods for sale or books in a library.

clue.text: Group of players groaned audibly

indicators.note: audibly means as heard, so the word is identified by its sound rather than its spelling

parts.note: to sigh is to let out a groan of weariness

explanation.surface: A team of players groaned loudly.
explanation.definitionFit: A side is a team, the group of players representing one party in a match.

clue.text: Cliff escape set abroad — this is what you expect in a Bond film

definitions.text: this is what you expect in a Bond film

indicators.note: abroad can mean astray or scattered widely, so the letters are spread into a new order

parts.note: taken as written

explanation.surface: A cliff-top getaway filmed on location overseas, typical of a James Bond movie.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Abroad' fits Bond's foreign locations so well that it reads as scene-setting, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Bond films are famous for spectacular stunts, explosions and visual trickery created by special effects teams.

clue.text: Green pistachio nuts cracked by Edward

indicators.note: by means beside, so the name's abbreviation sits next to the rearranged letters
something cracked is broken apart, so the letters of the nuts are broken up and rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
Ed is the short form of the name Edward

explanation.surface: Edward is cracking green pistachio nuts.
explanation.walkthrough: Pistachios really are green, so 'Green' looks like a description of the nuts rather than the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone green is naive and inexperienced, which is what unsophisticated means.

clue.text: Words from groom perhaps about one tense ass

indicators.note: about means around, so the groom's words go around the number

parts.note: 'I do' is what a groom says at the altar
I is the Roman numeral one
T is the grammatical abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A nervous groom's wedding vows, with a donkey for comic effect.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Ass' could be the donkey, but here it means a fool.
explanation.definitionFit: An ass is a stupid person, which is what an idiot is.

clue.text: Evicted criminal trapping Parisian and Maigret?

indicators.note: trapping means holding something inside, so the French word goes within the other letters
something criminal is crooked, so the letters are bent out of their order

parts.note: taken as written
et is French for 'and'

explanation.surface: A criminal who has been evicted is caught by a Parisian, with Maigret involved.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark marks Maigret, Simenon's French police inspector, as one example of the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Inspector Maigret is the fictional Paris police detective in Georges Simenon's novels.

clue.text: Some enjoy a lecture here?

indicators.note: some means only part of what follows, so the letters lie within the words

parts.note: the last letter of the first word, the middle word, and the start of the third

explanation.surface: A wry suggestion that some students actually like their lectures at this place.
explanation.walkthrough: The whole clue is both wordplay and definition: lectures happen at a university, and the question mark admits it is only one example.
explanation.definitionFit: Yale is an Ivy League university in Connecticut, a place where lectures are given.

clue.text: At university with jerk, pretentious and vulgar

parts.note: a British student at university is said to be up
a start is a sudden jerk of the body

explanation.surface: A description of an obnoxious university student.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Up' for being in residence at a university, especially Oxford or Cambridge, is a British usage.
explanation.definitionFit: An upstart is someone newly risen in status who behaves arrogantly, so as an adjective it means pretentious and vulgar.

clue.text: Keep going north after solo ride all over the place

indicators.note: after means coming later, so the compass letter is placed at the end
all over the place means in disorder, so the letters of the two words are scrambled

parts.note: taken as written
N is the abbreviation for north

explanation.surface: A rider persevering northwards after a chaotic solo journey.
explanation.definitionFit: To soldier on is to persevere doggedly despite difficulties, an idiom drawn from military endurance.

clue.text: Something used for wiping bum

definitions.meaning: first meaning: a soft absorbent pad for cleaning
second meaning: to cadge or scrounge from others

explanation.surface: Toilet humour: an item for cleaning one's backside.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Bum' reads as the British word for bottom, but it is the verb meaning to beg or scrounge.
explanation.definitionFit: A sponge is an absorbent cleaning pad, and to sponge off people is to bum things from them.

clue.text: Snakes, say, we spot regularly in nettles

indicators.note: in means placed inside, so the kept letters go within the other word

parts.note: nettles as a verb means irritates, as does riles

indicators.note: regularly means at even intervals, so every other letter of the words is kept

parts.note: the second, fourth and sixth letters

explanation.surface: We keep spotting snakes in the nettle patch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Nettles' reads as the plant where snakes hide; it is the verb meaning annoys.
explanation.definitionFit: Snakes are one kind of reptile, with lizards, turtles and crocodiles; 'say' marks them as an example.

clue.text: Rip off coat

definitions.meaning: first meaning: to overcharge or swindle someone
second meaning: a sheep's wool, or a warm fleecy jacket

explanation.surface: An instruction to tear off a coat.
explanation.definitionFit: To fleece someone is to cheat them of money, and a fleece is a sheep's woolly coat or a soft jacket.

clue.text: Go off base following former policeman

indicators.note: following means coming after, so the base letter is placed after the rest

parts.note: ex means former
Plod is British slang for a policeman, from the Noddy books
e is the base of natural logarithms

explanation.surface: A retired policeman leaves the station.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Go off base' reads as leaving a station; the definition ends at 'off' and 'base' is the mathematical constant e.
explanation.definitionFit: A bomb that goes off detonates, which is to explode.

clue.text: Frank's seeing that Republican leader in extremis

parts.note: since means because, or seeing that
R is the standard abbreviation for Republican

indicators.note: a leader goes first, so only the opening letter of the following word is wanted

parts.note: the first letter of extremis; 'in' simply locates the leader within that phrase

explanation.surface: A political observation that Frank is a Republican leader in dire straits.
explanation.walkthrough: Frank looks like a man's name; it is the adjective meaning honest, with 's standing for 'is'.
explanation.definitionFit: Being frank means speaking honestly and openly, which is what being sincere is.

clue.text: Child finally goes for good

indicators.note: finally points to the end, so only the closing letter of the next word is taken

parts.note: the final letter
pro means in favour of, or for
G is the abbreviation for good

explanation.surface: A child at last leaves home for good.
explanation.walkthrough: Sprog is British informal slang for a child.
explanation.definitionFit: A sprog is a jocular British word for a young child or baby.

clue.text: Quarrel — it turns very loud

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, so the short word is read backwards

parts.note: taken as written
ff, fortissimo, is the musical mark for very loud

explanation.surface: An argument that gets heated and noisy.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiff is a minor squabble, a petty quarrel between friends or partners.

clue.text: Standing by bloke next to hospital department

indicators.note: next to means placed alongside, so the final piece follows directly after

parts.note: per means by, as in per post
a bloke is a man
ENT is the ear, nose and throat department

explanation.surface: A man waiting beside a hospital department.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Standing' looks like the posture of the bloke, but it is the adjective, as in a standing army.
explanation.definitionFit: A standing arrangement is a lasting, fixed one, so standing and permanent are synonyms.

clue.text: Boob reflected in mirror, regrettably

indicators.note: a mirror reflection runs the other way, so the letters are read backwards
in means contained within, so the letters lie inside the following words

parts.note: the end of the first word and the start of the second

explanation.surface: Someone sadly sees an embarrassing flaw in the mirror.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boob' reads as part of the body seen in a mirror, but it is British slang for a blunder.
explanation.definitionFit: A boob is an informal word for a silly mistake or blunder.

clue.text: Old editor picked up special poems

parts.note: O is the abbreviation for old

indicators.note: in a down clue, picked up means lifted, so the letters read from the bottom upwards

parts.note: ed is the abbreviation for editor
S is the abbreviation for special

explanation.surface: A veteran editor chose some special poems.
explanation.definitionFit: Odes are lyric poems, usually addressed to a person or thing in an elevated style.

clue.text: BBC boss maybe later recording broadcast about Spain

indicators.note: about means surrounding, so the rearranged letters go around the country code
broadcast means scattered widely, as seed is sown, so the letters are thrown into a new order

parts.note: taken as written
E is the international vehicle code for Spain (España)

explanation.surface: A broadcasting chief perhaps plans a later recording about Spain.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Broadcast' fits the BBC so well it reads as part of the picture, not an anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: The director-general is the chief executive of the BBC; 'maybe' marks it as one example of such a post.

clue.text: Forbidding nurse bandaging hip

indicators.note: a bandage wraps around a wound, so the nurse's word wraps around the other

parts.note: a sister is a senior nurse in Britain
hip and in both mean fashionable

explanation.surface: A stern nurse dressing a patient's hip.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Hip' looks like the joint being bandaged but means trendy. In British hospitals a sister is a senior nurse.
explanation.definitionFit: Something forbidding looks threatening or ominous, which is a sense of sinister.

clue.text: They hold baps — bread is reduced

indicators.note: reduced means cut short, so the word loses its final letter

parts.note: bread and brass are both slang for money

explanation.surface: Bread rolls at a discount, with baps on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: Baps are British soft bread rolls, which matches 'bread', but here baps is slang for breasts; brass is northern English slang for money.
explanation.definitionFit: Bras are undergarments that support the breasts, jokingly called baps in British slang.
